summary:
Project Ares is a free, browser-based, two-player game where kids ages 7–12 run a Mars base for 10 Sols and learn the real trade-offs of deep-space survival. One player is the Flight Director on Earth, who reads real NASA DONKI solar storm records, decides which ones will reach Mars, and warns the crew in a message of only 10 words. The other is the Surface Astronaut, who cannot see the Sun and must spend four daily work slots on air, power, shielding, and science, where every action costs something. Storms arrive 3–5 Sols after they are spotted, matching NASA's model-predicted Mars arrival times, so players must prepare ahead. Before launch, teams pick modules under a mass limit, and after the mission a debrief explains exactly why it succeeded or failed, linking each storm to its real NASA record. DONKI data is real; the dose model and Mars conditions are simulated, and every element is labeled as real or simulated. No download or account needed: play it at

details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Project Ares is a two-role, turn-based Mars base game for kids ages 7–12. Players first build their base under a mass limit: 7 modules (solar array, battery, greenhouse, recycler, regolith shield, comms dish, and science lab), and they cannot take everything. Then they fly 10 Sols (Mars days). Each Sol, the Flight Director on Earth, reviews real NASA DONKI solar-storm records, decides which ones will reach Mars, and sends the astronaut a message of at most 10 words picked from a word bank. The surface Astronaut cannot see the Sun. They only see the base status and Earth's message, and spend 4 daily Work Slots on recycling, greenhouse, solar panels, shielding, shelter drills, or science. Every action costs power, so no choice is free. Storms arrive 3–5 Sols after they are spotted, using NASA's model-predicted Mars arrival times. After the mission, a debrief shows a 10-Sol timeline, each storm with its real NASA record link, a review of Earth's message, and the key turning points.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Kids experience real mission trade-offs instead of reading about them: power spent on science is not spent on air, and shielding built today costs tomorrow's battery. They also learn why forecasting, radiation shielding, and clear communication under tight limits matter for Moon-to-Mars exploration. It is free, runs in any browser, needs no account or download, and works on phones, so classrooms and families can use it right away. Failure is a lesson, not a punishment: the debrief explains exactly what happened and suggests what to try next.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks, no external requests, works offline); an SVG debrief chart; Node.js for 21 automated engine tests, Git and GitHub Pages for hosting. The game engine is deterministic with no random numbers, so every run of a scenario is reproducible and explainable. AI tools helped with design and coding (see the Super Intelligence section).

REAL DATA AND HONEST LABELS

Real: 12 NASA DONKI records (IDs, dates, speeds, and NASA's model-predicted Mars arrival), copied from the public DONKI pages as a snapshot. It is not a live feed, and the game says so. Simulated: the radiation dose model (dose adds up, never resets, and shielding wears out), the Mars conditions (thin air, no global magnetic field, dust haze cuts solar power), and all game balance. Every element is tagged REAL NASA DATA, SIMULATED (science-based), or SIMULATED (game), and an About the Data screen explains each one.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Asymmetric information: Earth sees the Sun but not your battery, and you see your battery but not the Sun. A 10-word limit forces the Flight Director to prioritize. Decoy storms that NASA's model says miss Mars make false alarms costly. Three scenarios (First Contact, Double Trouble, The Big One) use different real storms, so players can replay with new strategies.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Age: plain language, glossary pop-ups for words like Sol and CME, and big buttons for phones.

- Focus: three resources plus one dose gauge, rather than many systems, so kids can follow the trade-offs.

- Honesty: DONKI is the only real dataset because it needs no API and gives dated events. OSDR and Mars surface data are simulated and labeled, not claimed as used.

- Simplifications we disclose: real Earth–Mars signals take about 3–22 minutes, so we use a word limit and one-day-old telemetry. We treat 1 Sol as 1 Earth day, and very fast real storms use a 3-Sol minimum warning.

- Accessibility: keyboard play, readable contrast, and no information carried by color alone.
